lead: A pushdown automaton is a finite automaton with a stack, and it accepts exactly the context-free languages. This unit defines the machine, traces its runs with instantaneous descriptions, compares the deterministic and nondeterministic versions, and shows that it is the same as a context-free grammar. You finish able to build a PDA for a language, convert it to a grammar and back, and see where parsers come from.
about: Unit 4 adds one stack to the machines of Unit 1 and gets exactly the context-free languages. Chapter 4.1 defines the pushdown automaton and the instantaneous description used to trace a run move by move. Chapter 4.2 shows that accepting by final state and accepting by empty stack have the same power, and gives both conversions. Chapter 4.3 separates deterministic from nondeterministic machines and places the deterministic languages strictly inside the context-free ones. Chapter 4.4 proves the two-way equivalence with context-free grammars, working both conversions on small examples. Chapter 4.5, taught in only a few universities, reads those two conversions as top-down and bottom-up parsing. After the unit you can design a PDA for a language, convert it to a grammar and back, and trace a run ID by ID.

chapters.idea: A pushdown automaton is a finite control plus one unbounded stack, and the triple (state, unread input, stack contents) is everything you need to describe the run.
chapters.depth: Give the seven-tuple P = (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q₀, Z₀, F): Q states, Σ input alphabet, Γ stack alphabet, δ the transition function, q₀ the start state, Z₀ the initial stack symbol, F the final states. Define δ : Q × (Σ ∪ {ε}) × Γ → P(Q × Γ*) and explain the two outputs: the next state and the string pushed in place of the popped top. Read a transition (q, a, X) → (p, γ) as: in state q, reading a (or nothing if a = ε), with X on top, go to p and replace X by γ, written on the stack with its leftmost symbol on top. Some syllabi write the stack alphabet as Γ and others as Z or Π; the stack itself is also called the pushdown store or the pushdown list. Define the instantaneous description (ID) as (q, w, γ): q is the current state, w the input still to read, γ the whole stack with the top at the left. Define the single-move relation ⊢ and its reflexive-transitive closure ⊢*. Show the transition diagram convention: an arrow labelled a, X / γ. Keep it to definition plus tracing; no new language theory here.
chapters.figure: blocks, direction right, 3 nodes: 'Input tape' with note 'a a b b, read left to right' (normal), 'Finite control' with note 'state q, table δ' (accent), 'Stack' with note 'top Z₀, then A A' (live); edges input→control 'read one symbol', control→stack 'push / pop top', and a dashed edge stack→control 'top symbol'. Shows the three parts of a PDA and the loop that makes the stack readable by the control.
chapters.example: Let P = ({q₀,q₁,q₂}, {a,b}, {Z₀,A}, δ, q₀, Z₀, {q₂}) with δ(q₀,a,Z₀) = {(q₀,AZ₀)}, δ(q₀,a,A) = {(q₀,AA)}, δ(q₀,b,A) = {(q₁,ε)}, δ(q₁,b,A) = {(q₁,ε)}, δ(q₁,ε,Z₀) = {(q₂,Z₀)}, all other entries empty. Trace the IDs for input aabb. Answer: (q₀,aabb,Z₀) ⊢ (q₀,abb,AZ₀) ⊢ (q₀,bb,AAZ₀) ⊢ (q₁,b,AZ₀) ⊢ (q₁,ε,Z₀) ⊢ (q₂,ε,Z₀), so aabb is accepted. Also state the language: L(P) = {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 1}.
chapters.trap: Writing the stack in the ID with the top at the right. The top is the leftmost symbol of γ, so pushing A on Z₀ gives AZ₀, never Z₀A. The second trap is reading δ as a single move: δ returns a set of (state, stack string) pairs, and one entry can be a set of size 0, 1 or more.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for DFA and NFA definitions, transition tables and the idea of an extended transition function.
chapters.leave: The two acceptance conventions go to 4.2; the deterministic case to 4.3; the grammar link to 4.4.

chapters.idea: Final state and empty stack are two ways of saying 'accept', and each one can be simulated by the other, so they accept exactly the same languages.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this as its own topic, so keep it short and concrete. Final state acceptance: w ∈ L(P) if (q₀, w, Z₀) ⊢* (q, ε, γ) for some q ∈ F and any γ. Empty stack acceptance, also called acceptance by null stack or empty store: (q₀, w, Z₀) ⊢* (q, ε, ε) for any state q. State both conversions as lemmas. Final state to empty stack: add a new bottom marker X₀ not in Γ, add a new start state q₀′ with δ(q₀′,ε,X₀) = {(q₀, Z₀X₀)}, and from every final state add moves into a new erasing state that pops the whole stack. Empty stack to final state: add X₀ and a new start state that pushes Z₀ above it, then one new final state entered exactly when X₀ becomes the top. Give the direction of the proof only as 'the new machine copies each move of the old one'; do not prove language equality in full.
chapters.figure: blocks, direction down, 5 nodes: 'P accepts by final state' (normal) → 'new start q₀′ pushes X₀Z₀' (accent) → 'simulate every move of P' (normal) → 'final state: enter eraser' (live) → 'eraser pops all, stack empty' (accent), with a dashed back edge from the last node to the eraser node labelled 'while stack non-empty'. Shows that the conversion only wraps the old machine and adds a loop that empties the stack.
chapters.example: Take the PDA of 4.1, which accepts aabb in final state q₂. Apply the final-state-to-empty-stack construction and trace the same input. New machine: states q₀′, q₀, q₁, q₂, qe; stack alphabet {X₀, Z₀, A}; δ(q₀′,ε,X₀) = {(q₀, Z₀X₀)}; δ(q₂,ε,Y) = {(qe,ε)} for Y in {X₀, Z₀, A}; δ(qe,ε,Y) = {(qe,ε)} for the same Y; all old moves kept. Trace: (q₀′,aabb,X₀) ⊢ (q₀,aabb,Z₀X₀) ⊢* (q₂,ε,Z₀X₀) ⊢ (qe,ε,X₀) ⊢ (qe,ε,ε). Accepted by empty stack.
chapters.trap: Using a new bottom marker that already belongs to Γ. The simulated machine must never see X₀ or it will pop it and change its own behaviour. Second trap: letting the eraser run before the machine has finished, that is, adding erase moves out of non-final states.
chapters.prereq: 4.1 for the seven-tuple, the move relation and ID notation.
chapters.leave: Whether the machine is deterministic is 4.3; the grammar equivalence is 4.4.

chapters.idea: A PDA is deterministic when no configuration offers a choice; nondeterministic PDAs accept all context-free languages, deterministic ones accept only a strictly smaller family.
chapters.depth: Define the DPDA, sometimes written deterministic pushdown automaton: for every state q, input symbol a and stack symbol X there is at most one move, and if δ(q,ε,X) is non-empty then δ(q,a,X) must be empty for every a. That second clause is the part students forget. The ordinary PDA from 4.1 is now called an NPDA, nondeterministic pushdown automaton. State the three facts without full proofs: NPDAs accept exactly the context-free languages (proved in 4.4); every DPDA language is a CFL; some CFLs are not accepted by any DPDA. Name that smaller family the deterministic context-free languages, DCFLs, and note two consequences: DCFLs are closed under complement while CFLs are not, and a DCFL can be parsed in time proportional to the input length. Give the standard example of a CFL that is not a DCFL: L = {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 1} ∪ {aⁿb²ⁿ : n ≥ 1}.
chapters.figure: sets, nested, outermost first: set 'CFL (NPDA)' with item '{aⁿbⁿ} ∪ {aⁿb²ⁿ}', set 'DCFL (DPDA)' with item '{aⁿbⁿ}', set 'Regular' with item 'a*b*'. Shows the strict chain regular ⊂ DCFL ⊂ CFL and puts one language in each ring.
chapters.example: Build a DPDA for {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 1} and then try to extend it to {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 1} ∪ {aⁿb²ⁿ : n ≥ 1}. The DPDA: δ(q₀,a,Z₀) = (q₀,AZ₀), δ(q₀,a,A) = (q₀,AA), δ(q₀,b,A) = (q₁,ε), δ(q₁,b,A) = (q₁,ε), δ(q₁,ε,Z₀) = (q₂,Z₀), with q₂ final; every entry is single-valued and no (q,X) pair has both an ε-move and an input move. For the union, at the very first b the machine must already know whether to pop one A per b or one A per two b's, and both cases start with the same input prefix aⁿb, so it has to guess. A DPDA cannot guess, so no DPDA accepts the union.
chapters.trap: Calling a PDA deterministic because the table looks small. Check both conditions: one entry per triple, and no ε-move sitting beside an input move for the same (q, X).
chapters.prereq: 4.1 for the machine, 4.2 for the acceptance conventions used in the definitions.
chapters.leave: Closure and pumping properties of CFLs stay in Unit 3. Which grammars give deterministic parsers is 4.5.

chapters.idea: Every context-free grammar becomes a PDA that keeps the unexpanded part of a leftmost derivation on its stack, and every PDA becomes a grammar whose variables mean 'go from state p to state q and remove A from the stack'.
chapters.depth: Both directions, with the constructions written out as recipes. CFG to PDA: use one state q plus the initial symbol Z₀; start with δ(q,ε,Z₀) = {(q, S Z₀)}; for each production A → α add δ(q,ε,A) = {(q, αᴿ)}, pushing the reverse so the leftmost symbol of α lands on top; for each terminal a add δ(q,a,a) = {(q,ε)}. The result accepts by empty stack exactly the grammar's language, and simulating it is a leftmost derivation. PDA to CFG: first say every PDA can be rewritten as a simple PDA (one state, empty stack acceptance, each move either pushes one symbol or pops one), then introduce the variable [p A q], meaning 'from state p with A on top, reach state q with A gone'. Give the two forms of production: [p A q] → a [p′ B₁ r₁] [r₁ B₂ r₂] … for a push move and [p A q] → a for a pop move. Say the resulting grammar has many useless variables and needs the simplification steps from Unit 3. Mention that this pair of constructions is the standard proof that PDAs and CFGs describe the same languages.
chapters.figure: array, 6 rows, title 'One-state PDA running S → aSb | ε on input ab'. Each row is one move; cells hold the stack written bottom to top with Z₀ leftmost, the row label is the input still unread, and the marked cell is the current top. Rows: (label ab, cells Z₀ S, top marked), (label ab, cells Z₀ b S a, new top marked), (label b, cells Z₀ b S, top marked), (label b, cells Z₀ b, top marked as the expansion S → ε happens), (label ε, cells Z₀ S? no: cells Z₀, top marked), (label ε, cells empty, shown as one ε cell). Shows the stack growing while expanding and shrinking while matching.
chapters.example: Grammar S → aSb | ε, input ab, one-state PDA accepting by empty stack with bottom marker Z₀. Trace: (q,ab,Z₀) ⊢ (q,ab,SZ₀) [push S] ⊢ (q,ab,bSaZ₀) [S → aSb, reversed] ⊢ (q,b,SaZ₀) [match a] ⊢ (q,b,baZ₀)? no: after matching a the stack is b S Z₀, then S → ε gives b Z₀, then matching b gives Z₀, then popping Z₀ gives empty stack. Answer list: Z₀S, Z₀bSa, Z₀bS, Z₀b, Z₀, ε with inputs ab, ab, b, b, ε, ε. Accepted.
chapters.trap: Pushing the right-hand side in the order written. Push its reverse, or the grammar's strings come out backwards and the PDA rejects them. Second trap: forgetting that the grammar built by the PDA-to-CFG construction is full of unreachable variables — the language is right but the grammar needs simplifying.
chapters.prereq: 4.1 for the machine, Unit 3 for productions, derivations, leftmost derivations and grammar simplification.
chapters.leave: Normal forms, ambiguity and the CYK algorithm stay in Unit 3. How the same construction becomes a compiler parser is 4.5.

chapters.idea: A parser is a PDA in disguise: a top-down parser predicts a leftmost derivation starting from the start symbol, a bottom-up parser shifts input and reduces handles to rebuild the parse tree from the leaves.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this unit as an overview, so keep it to the shape of the two methods and one worked sequence each, no table construction. Top-down: begin with the start symbol on the stack, replace a nonterminal by a production body, match terminals against the input; also called predictive or recursive-descent parsing. It needs the grammar without left recursion and without common prefixes, which is why LL(1) grammars are named. Bottom-up: move input symbols onto a stack (shift), and whenever the top of the stack matches the body of a production, replace it by the head (reduce); the sequence of reductions is a rightmost derivation read backwards. Name the LR family, SLR and LALR, as the table-driven bottom-up methods, and note that a conflict in the table means that grammar is not handled by that method. Tie back: 4.4 supplies the engine, 4.3 explains why only some grammars are deterministic. Note the everyday use: compilers and parser generators.
chapters.figure: tree, shape box, root E with note 'expand 1'. Children: E (note 'expand 2'), '+' (note 'match'), T (note 'expand 3'). The left E has child T (note 'expand 4') whose child F (note 'expand 5') has child id (note 'reduce F→id first'). The right T has children T (note 'expand 6'), '*' (note 'match') and F (note 'expand 8') with child id (note 'reduce last'). The middle T has child F (note 'expand 7') with child id (note 'reduce before *'). Shows the parse tree of id + id * id with the top-down expansion order on the internal nodes and the bottom-up reduction order at the leaves.
chapters.example: Grammar E → E + T | T, T → T * F | F, F → id. For input id + id * id give both orders. Top-down, leftmost: E ⇒ E + T ⇒ T + T ⇒ F + T ⇒ id + T ⇒ id + T * F ⇒ id + F * F ⇒ id + id * F ⇒ id + id * id; the productions used in order are E→E+T, E→T, T→F, F→id, T→T*F, T→F, F→id, F→id. Bottom-up, shift-reduce: shift id, reduce F→id, T→F, E→T; shift +; shift id, reduce F→id, T→F; shift *; shift id, reduce F→id; reduce T→T*F; reduce E→E+T. Both build the same tree.
chapters.trap: Feeding the grammar as written to a top-down parser. Left recursion such as E → E + T makes recursive descent call itself forever; the rule must be removed before the parser is built, and bottom-up methods are the ones that tolerate it.
chapters.prereq: 4.4 for the grammar-to-PDA construction, Unit 3 for derivations and parse trees.
chapters.leave: LL(1) table filling, FIRST and FOLLOW sets, and LR item sets belong to a compilers course. Ambiguity stays in Unit 3.
